clue.text: The scornful lady's gentlewoman

parts.note: points to the waiting-woman in Beaumont and Fletcher's comedy The Scornful Lady, whose name became a general word for a lady's maid

explanation.walkthrough: The Scornful Lady is a Jacobean comedy by Beaumont and Fletcher; its maid's name passed into English as a word for a personal servant.
explanation.definitionFit: The waiting-gentlewoman in The Scornful Lady bears this name, which later became a common noun for any lady's maid.

clue.text: Gap author possibly found in signed copy

indicators.note: possibly says these two words may be rearranged into some other form

explanation.surface: A missing author is tracked down by way of a copy bearing a signature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' tells you to rearrange the nine letters of GAP AUTHOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A signed copy carries the writer's own handwritten signature on its flyleaf.

clue.text: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read

definitions.text: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read

parts.words: Sarah, gift of Isis and a fantastic read
parts.note: the surname of the fantasy novelist Sarah ..., which as a Greek name means given by the goddess Isis, and whose books are fantasy reading

explanation.surface: A woman called Sarah, a present from the goddess, and a novel full of wonders.
explanation.walkthrough: Three hints to one name: the American fantasy writer Sarah Isidore, the Greek name's meaning 'gift of Isis', and 'a fantastic read' for her fantasy fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek personal name means 'gift of Isis', and it is also the surname of a fantasy author called Sarah.

clue.text: Poetic measure of those opposed to former times

parts.note: antis are people against something
the past is former times

explanation.surface: A verse foot favoured by people who resist anything old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: An antispast is a metrical foot of four syllables, short-long-long-short, used in classical prosody.

clue.text: Reported bloomer affected writer

indicators.note: reported means the word for the flower is to be taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a lily is a flower, something that blooms

explanation.surface: A rumoured gaffe is said to have hit an author hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' looks like a blunder, but here it is a flower. John Lyly's elaborate prose style, Euphuism, made 'affected' his trademark.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lyly, Elizabethan author of Euphues, wrote in a famously mannered, ornate style.

clue.text: Bad actor in single combat awarded Prix Goncourt

indicators.note: in places the bad actor within the word for single combat

parts.note: a duel is combat between two people
a ham is an overacting performer

explanation.surface: A poor performer in a swordfight scene still wins France's top literary prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Georges Duhamel won the Prix Goncourt in 1918 for Civilisation.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist Georges Duhamel received the Goncourt, France's leading prize for fiction, in 1918.

clue.text: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?

definitions.text: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?

parts.words: Did he bracket World War I, this author to keep up with?
parts.note: 'bracket' hints at a war book titled for a parenthesis, and 'keep up with' at the idiom about keeping pace with one's neighbours, whose surname this writer shares

explanation.walkthrough: In Parenthesis (1937) is a long poem about World War I; 'bracket' stands for parenthesis, and 'keep up with' recalls 'keeping up with the Joneses'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Welsh poet-painter wrote In Parenthesis about the trenches, and his surname is the one in 'keeping up with the' neighbours idiom.

clue.text: In another sense, 13 may make haste

indicators.note: may make says the letters of the word haste can be formed into a different word

explanation.surface: A clue cross-referring to entry 13, suggesting it might speed things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is ANATHEMATA, votive offerings there; in its other sense an anathema is a thing cursed or loathed. 'may make' rearranges HASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is something detested or cursed, so the plural relates to loathing.

clue.text: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant

definitions.text: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant

parts.words: A tragic adaptation of D' Avenant
parts.note: Sir William D'Avenant made a Restoration version of one of Shakespeare's tragedies

explanation.walkthrough: William D'Avenant, poet laureate, adapted Shakespeare's Scottish tragedy with songs and spectacle in the 1660s.
explanation.definitionFit: D'Avenant's operatic rewrite of the Scottish play held the stage for decades after 1664.

clue.text: Platonic dialogue with a tart upset Aristophanes comedy

indicators.note: the dialogue with the extra letters added makes the comedy, so the comedy minus those letters gives the dialogue

parts.note: Lysistrata is Aristophanes' play about a sex strike

indicators.note: upset means the words a tart are turned upside down, read backwards in a down light

explanation.surface: A philosophical text paired with a loose woman turns into a Greek comic play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns A TART into TRATA; the dialogue plus TRATA is LYSISTRATA, so the comedy less TRATA leaves the dialogue.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato's Lysis is a short Socratic dialogue on friendship.

clue.text: Dickens hero wants another card?

definitions.meaning: Oliver, the workhouse boy who asks for more
in pontoon, saying '...' asks the dealer for one more card

explanation.walkthrough: Pontoon is the British name for blackjack; 'twist' there means 'hit me'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver of the Dickens novel bears this surname, and in the card game pontoon (blackjack) this word requests a further card.

clue.text: Italian writer is cut, unfortunately, from old law book

parts.note: Primo Levi, the Italian author of If This Is a Man

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the letters of 'is cut' have come out badly jumbled

explanation.surface: An Italian author's work is sadly cut from an ancient legal text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' is the anagram signal for 'is cut'; 'from' only links the wordplay to the Biblical definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The third book of the Pentateuch sets out the priestly laws of ancient Israel.

clue.text: Describes work with many explanatory notes?

definitions.text: Describes work with many explanatory notes?

parts.words: Describes work with many explanatory notes?
parts.note: a gloss is a marginal explanatory note, so a text full of them would be described by the adjective formed from it, which normally means shiny

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective usually means shiny or slick, but read as 'full of glosses' it suits an annotated text.

clue.text: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist

definitions.text: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist

parts.words: It's all Greek for Joyce protagonist
parts.note: Joyce's Ulysses takes its title from the Latin form of the Homeric hero's name, so the original Greek form is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'It's all Greek' looks like the idiom for incomprehensible, but literally asks for the Greek name of Joyce's title figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses is the Latin name for the Homeric wanderer; the Greek form is the one Homer used.

clue.text: Some votive offerings of 5

parts.note: the Greek word for things set up as offerings to a god is also the title of a long poem by the writer at 5

explanation.walkthrough: 5 is DAVID JONES, whose long poem has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek plural for things dedicated to a deity is the title of David Jones's 1952 poem.

clue.text: De Sade laughingly includes Forster heroine

indicators.note: includes says the answer sits inside the run of the words before it

explanation.surface: The Marquis, chuckling, adds one of E. M. Forster's women to his cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' points to the letters hidden across dE SADE LAughingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Adela Quested is the young Englishwoman at the centre of A Passage to India.

clue.text: Like the Houses of Parliament, or new black letter?

parts.note: neo- is the prefix for new
black letter is the heavy medieval typeface also called Gothic

explanation.surface: Is the Westminster building styled like a fresh dark typeface?
explanation.walkthrough: The Palace of Westminster, London's Houses of Parliament, was rebuilt in the 19th century in a revived medieval style.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry and Pugin's Westminster palace is the classic example of Victorian revival of medieval architecture.

clue.text: Mackenzie's idea of where we live

definitions.text: Mackenzie's idea of where we live

parts.words: Mackenzie's idea of where we live
parts.note: Compton Mackenzie wrote a novel whose title is a phrase naming the road one lives on

explanation.walkthrough: Compton Mackenzie, author of Whisky Galore, also wrote this book.
explanation.definitionFit: Compton Mackenzie's 1931 novel takes its title from a homely phrase for one's home road.

clue.text: Stephen King book, richest in rewrite

indicators.note: rewrite tells you to set down the letters of the preceding words in a new order

explanation.surface: A Stephen King novel, among the most lucrative, gets revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is part of the fodder, not a link: the nine letters of RICHEST IN rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: King's 1983 horror novel is about a possessed 1958 Plymouth Fury car.

clue.text: Name of section (like Bleak or Lear?)

definitions.text: Name of section (like Bleak or Lear?)

parts.words: Name of section (like Bleak or Lear?)
parts.note: each of the two words is part of a longer book or play title, Bleak House and King Lear, and the book term for a short title page fits both

explanation.definitionFit: In bookmaking, the short title printed on a page before the main title page, or heading a section, has this name.

clue.text: Bloom, perhaps, formerly on Belgian throne

definitions.meaning: Joyce's Bloom has this first name in Ulysses
three past kings of Belgium bore this name

explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses' Mr Bloom shares a first name with three Belgian monarchs.

clue.text: Versifier, say, who took a short view of Othello

definitions.text: who took a short view of Othello

indicators.note: say signals that the word for a versifier is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a rhymer is a composer of verse

explanation.surface: A poet, perhaps, who was brief and dismissive about Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Rymer's A Short View of Tragedy (1693) famously mocked Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Rymer, Restoration critic, attacked Shakespeare's Moor play in his 1693 treatise.

clue.text: A version of Roma, by way of La Romana's creator

indicators.note: a version of means the next word appears in a changed letter order

parts.note: via means by way of

explanation.surface: Another form of the Italian capital's name leads to the author of a Roman novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A version of' is the anagram signal for 'Roma'. La Romana (The Woman of Rome) is a 1947 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Alberto Moravia wrote the 1947 novel La Romana (The Woman of Rome).

clue.text: He knew Cressida better than Troilus

definitions.text: He knew Cressida better than Troilus

parts.words: He knew Cressida better than Troilus
parts.note: 'knew' in the biblical sense: the Greek warrior to whom Cressida transfers her love in the camp

explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare and Chaucer, Cressida abandons Troilus for this Greek hero.

clue.text: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)

definitions.text: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)

parts.words: "Tired of digging up potatoes, and spudding up " (Thomas Hardy)
parts.note: a quotation from Hardy with its last word missing, a kind of weed one cuts out with a spud

explanation.definitionFit: Dock is a broad-leaved weed that farmhands dug out with a narrow spade called a spud.

clue.text: It has always supported art

parts.note: 'supported' literally: the stand that holds a painter's canvas

explanation.definitionFit: A painter's frame stand physically holds up the canvas while work is done.

clue.text: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life

definitions.text: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life

parts.words: Anita Brookner and Alan Sillitoe offered them in life
parts.note: both novelists wrote a book titled A ... in Life, so between them they offered two of these

explanation.definitionFit: Brookner's first novel and a Sillitoe novel are each called A Start in Life, giving two beginnings.

clue.text: River goddess

definitions.meaning: the Thames at Oxford is known by this name
the Egyptian goddess, wife of Osiris

explanation.walkthrough: The Thames is called this as it flows through Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford stretch of the Thames shares its name with the Egyptian mother goddess.

clue.text: Irritable habits of Meredith's girl?

parts.note: cross means irritable
ways are habits, as in set in one's ways

explanation.surface: A girl in a Meredith novel has bad-tempered manners.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's heroine is Diana of the Crossways, so the girl is identified by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel Diana of the Crossways names its heroine by this place.

clue.text: Poetic PS

parts.note: a postscript to a poem: the short closing stanza addressed to a patron, as in a ballade

explanation.definitionFit: The short final stanza of a ballade acts as an afterthought or dedication.

clue.text: Seating arrangement in church is ideal, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps implies the letters of 'is ideal' may form something else

explanation.surface: The pews at church are laid out perfectly, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS IDEAL; 'arrangement' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedilia are the row of stone seats for clergy set into the south wall of a chancel.

clue.text: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)

definitions.text: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)

parts.words: "As a painter would a beggar under a triumphal arch" (W. S. Landor)
parts.note: a Landor quotation lacking its verb, meaning to place or position a figure

explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to place or position, as an artist sets a figure in a scene.
